section_summary: This section comprises diplomatic records of the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo from April through July 1935, primarily consisting of regular monthly political reports and attached transmittal lists of despatches and telegrams. It documents major international issues involving Japan, including Western protests over the Manchukuo oil monopoly and the domestic Petroleum Industry Law, Japanese military pressure in North China, Soviet-Japanese boundary and fishery frictions, and tariff disputes with Canada and Egypt. Domestically, the reports highlight the political and institutional campaign against Dr. Tatsukichi Minobe's constitutional 'organ theory' of the Emperor, Cabinet structural reforms such as the creation of the Cabinet Deliberative Body, and key personnel shake-ups within the Imperial Japanese Army and the South Manchuria Railway.

subfiles.about: The concluding portion of the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report on political, international, and economic conditions in Japan during April 1935.
subfiles.summary: This document contains the final sections of the Tokyo Embassy's monthly political and economic report for April 1935. It examines Japanese diplomatic ties with Siam, Western objections to the Manchukuo oil monopoly, and potential diplomatic recognition of Manchukuo by Belgium and the Dominican Republic, alongside Soviet negotiations over North Saghalien and northern fisheries. On the domestic front, it records the formation of the National Policy Investigation Council, the government crackdown on Dr. Tatsukichi Minobe's constitutional theory of the Emperor, and reactionary threats against Prince Saionji. It also reviews trade figures, efforts to expand imports from Latin America to prevent tariff restrictions, and the Foreign Office's official adoption of the term 'East Asia' in lieu of 'Far East', followed by lists of despatches sent during April.
subfiles.title: Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of April, 1935

subfiles.about: Comprehensive monthly political and economic report on conditions in Japan for May 1935 transmitted by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew.
subfiles.summary: This monthly report covers American-Japanese affairs during May 1935, including Admiral Upham's visit aboard the USS Augusta, agitation in Japan by Filipino Sakdalista leader Benigno Ramos, the detention and fine of retired U.S. Navy officer William S. Gates in Taiwan, and the foreign oil companies' impasse with the Manchukuo monopoly. Regional developments feature the Japanese military garrison's ultimatum at Tientsin following the elevation of the Japanese Legation in China to an embassy, Japan's formal denunciation of the 1928 fisheries convention with Soviet Russia, and border talks at Manchuli. Internal affairs highlight the establishment of the Cabinet Deliberative Body and Cabinet Investigation Bureau, the political break between the Minseito and Seiyukai parties, and growing military pressure against liberal constitutional views. The subfile concludes with complete lists of Embassy despatches and telegrams sent to the State Department during May.
subfiles.title: Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of May, 1935 (Report No. 104)

subfiles.about: Internal Department of State charge slip indicating the withdrawal of file materials by the Division of Far Eastern Affairs.
subfiles.summary: Charge slip records a document checked out to Far Eastern Affairs by clerks CFH and Amrine, marking the missing June 1935 monthly report's filing gap.
subfiles.title: Department of State Charge Slip

subfiles.about: The first sixteen pages of the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report on Japanese political, diplomatic, and economic affairs for July 1935.
subfiles.summary: This report reviews relations between the United States and Japan during July 1935, discussing foreign oil firms under the Petroleum Industry Law, the departure of Ambassador Joseph C. Grew on home leave, the commemoration of General Grant's death, and Japanese reactions to American Pacific naval policies and textile processing tax proposals. In external affairs, it analyzes the settlement of the Chinese 'Hsin Sheng' lèse-majesté incident, Japanese pressure toward an autonomous North China bloc, the creation of the Japan-Manchukuo Joint Economic Commission, tariff retaliation against Canada, and Egyptian treaty abrogation. It further details Soviet-Manchukuo border skirmishes, the stalled Manchuli conference with Outer Mongolia, fisheries negotiations in Moscow, and Japanese diplomatic ambiguities regarding the Italo-Ethiopian crisis, alongside the dismissal of General Jinzaburo Masaki as Inspector General of Military Education.
subfiles.title: Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of July, 1935 (Report No. 106)
